title: ALD Oxidant as A Tuning Knob for Memory Window Expansion in Ferroelectric FETs for Vertical NAND Applications
summary: Dielectric inserts are widely used to expand the memory window (MW) in ferroelectric FETs (FeFETs) for vertical NAND applications, with prior efforts focused primarily on material selection and stack positioning. Here, we demonstrate that the ALD oxidant used for the Al2O3 interlayer serves as a process-level tuning knob for MW engineering. H2O-grown Al2O3 yields a significantly larger MW (7-8 V) compared to O3 (4 V) for both gate-injection (12/3) and tunnel dielectric (8/3/8) configurations. While the tunnel dielectric (8/3/8) stack maintains robust retention up to 1e4s at 125C despite the larger MW, the gate-injection (12/3) configuration exhibits pronounced retention degradation for the H2O case. The enhanced MW is attributed to higher interlayer leakage associated with H2O-based ALD. These results establish oxidant choice as a key process parameter for co-optimizing MW and retention in ferroelectric NAND technologies.

AI.tldr: ALD oxidant choice (H2O vs O3) for Al2O3 interlayer significantly impacts memory window in FeFETs, with H2O providing larger MW but affecting retention differently depending on stack configuration.
AI.motivation: Prior work on dielectric inserts for FeFET memory window expansion focused on material selection and stack positioning, but oxidant choice in ALD processes was unexplored as a tuning parameter for MW engineering.
AI.method: Compared H2O-grown vs O3-grown Al2O3 interlayers in ferroelectric FETs using two configurations: gate-injection (12/3) and tunnel dielectric (8/3/8) stacks, evaluating memory window and retention characteristics.
AI.result: H2O-grown Al2O3 yields significantly larger memory window (7-8 V) compared to O3 (4 V) for both configurations. Tunnel dielectric stack maintains robust retention up to 1e4s at 125°C despite larger MW, while gate-injection configuration shows pronounced retention degradation with H2O.
AI.conclusion: ALD oxidant choice is a key process parameter for co-optimizing memory window and retention in ferroelectric NAND technologies, with enhanced MW attributed to higher interlayer leakage associated with H2O-based ALD.

title: Endohedral Derivatives of the Recently Synthesized Two-Dimensional Fullerene Networks: Electronic and Optical Insights from First-Principles Calculations
summary: The quasi-hexagonal phase of the two-dimensional fullerene network (qHPC$_{60}$), recently synthesized, has emerged as a stable carbon-based material with distinct structural and electronic features. In this work, we employed density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate the electronic and optical properties of its endohedral derivatives. The encapsulation of nitrogen, cerium, and strontium atoms inside fullerene cages was systematically analyzed at different concentrations. Our results show that encapsulation preserves the semiconducting backbone of pristine qHPC$_{60}$ while introducing localized electronic states that alter the bandgap and enable new transition channels. Nitrogen encapsulation produces intragap states with potential relevance for discrete optical emission, whereas cerium and strontium generate intraband states near the conduction edge. These modifications induce a red shift of the absorption onset into the visible spectrum, accompanied by enhanced refractive and absorptive responses. The robustness of the electronic structure under reduced concentrations indicates that the fully encapsulated limit adequately represents the system. Overall, the findings highlight impurity-endowed qHPC$_{60}$ as a promising platform for optoelectronic and light-harvesting applications.

AI.tldr: DFT study shows endohedral doping (N, Ce, Sr) of quasi-hexagonal 2D fullerene network preserves semiconducting backbone while introducing localized states that modify bandgap and optical properties, enabling visible-light absorption for optoelectronic applications.
AI.motivation: To investigate how endohedral encapsulation of different atoms (N, Ce, Sr) affects the electronic and optical properties of the recently synthesized quasi-hexagonal phase of 2D fullerene network (qHPC60), exploring its potential for optoelectronic applications.
AI.method: Employed density functional theory (DFT) calculations to systematically analyze electronic and optical properties of endohedral derivatives with nitrogen, cerium, and strontium atoms encapsulated inside fullerene cages at different concentrations.
AI.result: Encapsulation preserves semiconducting backbone while introducing localized electronic states: nitrogen creates intragap states for discrete optical emission; cerium and strontium generate intraband states near conduction edge. These modifications cause red shift of absorption onset into visible spectrum with enhanced refractive and absorptive responses. Electronic structure remains robust at reduced concentrations.
AI.conclusion: Impurity-endowed qHPC60 represents a promising platform for optoelectronic and light-harvesting applications due to preserved semiconducting properties combined with tunable electronic states and enhanced visible-light absorption capabilities.

title: Intertwined Swirling Polarization States in BaTiO$_3$ with Embedded BaZrO$_3$ Nanoregions
comment: Accepted for publication in Phys. Rev. Lett
summary: Ferroelectric materials embedded with dielectric inclusions offer a unique platform for exploring novel topological polar textures. Using first-principles-based atomistic simulations, we investigate the polarization behavior of a BaTiO$_3$ matrix containing segregated BaZrO$_3$ nanoregions. We demonstrate that the polar texture in three-dimensionally ordered arrays of dielectric inclusions is governed by their size and spacing, revealing three distinct regimes. At large separations, the nanocomposite exhibits bulk-like BaTiO3 phase transitions, while at smaller spacings, interconnected swirling polarization patterns give rise to vortex supercrystal states. We analyze the stabilization mechanisms of these states and show that each regime is characterized by distinct switching behavior. Furthermore, we find that nanocomposites with randomly distributed dielectric inclusions exhibit swirling polarization textures, giving rise to an amorphous network of entangled vortices. Our findings provide new insights into the physics of relaxor ferroelectrics, are consistent with recent experimental observations, and open up new possibilities for designing materials with emergent topological functionalities.

AI.tldr: BaTiO3 matrix with BaZrO3 dielectric inclusions exhibits three polarization regimes based on inclusion size/spacing: bulk-like behavior at large separations, vortex supercrystals at intermediate spacing, and amorphous vortex networks in random distributions.
AI.motivation: To explore novel topological polar textures in ferroelectric-dielectric nanocomposites and understand the physics of relaxor ferroelectrics through controlled dielectric inclusions.
AI.method: First-principles-based atomistic simulations of BaTiO3 matrix containing segregated BaZrO3 nanoregions, analyzing both ordered arrays and random distributions of dielectric inclusions.
AI.result: Three distinct regimes identified: 1) bulk-like BaTiO3 phase transitions at large separations, 2) interconnected swirling polarization patterns forming vortex supercrystal states at smaller spacings, 3) amorphous network of entangled vortices in randomly distributed inclusions.
AI.conclusion: Polar texture in ferroelectric-dielectric nanocomposites is governed by inclusion size and spacing, providing insights into relaxor ferroelectrics and enabling design of materials with emergent topological functionalities.

title: Bias in Universal Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials and its Effects on Fine-Tuning
summary: Universal machine learned interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) embody a growing area of interest due to their transferability across the periodic table, displaying an error of about 0.6 kcal/mol against the Matbench Discovery test set. However, we show that achieving more accurate predictions on out-of-domain tasks requires fine-tuning. Additionally, we investigate the existence and influence of model biases in molecular dynamics (MD) by examining two approaches for data generation: from multiple MD trajectories in parallel, which we call naive fine-tuning, and from a single MD trajectory with fine-tuning after set intervals, which we call periodic fine-tuning. Our results find that naive fine-tuning generates constrained datasets that fail to represent MD simulations, and thus downstream fine-tuned models fail during extrapolation. In contrast, periodic fine-tuning yields models which are more generalizable and accurate, producing low-error dynamics. These findings indicate the role of uMLIP bias in fine-tuning, and highlights the need for multiple fine-tuning steps. Lastly, we relate unphysical behavior to principal component space, and quantify extrapolations through Q-residual analysis, which are useful as a proxy for epistemic uncertainty for larger simulations.

AI.tldr: Universal MLIPs achieve ~0.6 kcal/mol error but require fine-tuning for out-of-domain accuracy; periodic fine-tuning outperforms naive fine-tuning by generating more generalizable models with lower error dynamics.
AI.motivation: Universal machine-learned interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) show good transferability but have limitations in out-of-domain accuracy, requiring investigation of fine-tuning approaches and model biases in molecular dynamics simulations.
AI.method: Compare two fine-tuning approaches: naive fine-tuning (from multiple parallel MD trajectories) vs. periodic fine-tuning (from single MD trajectory with interval-based fine-tuning). Analyze model biases, use principal component space to identify unphysical behavior, and apply Q-residual analysis for epistemic uncertainty quantification.
AI.result: Naive fine-tuning produces constrained datasets that fail to represent MD simulations, leading to poor extrapolation. Periodic fine-tuning yields more generalizable and accurate models with low-error dynamics. Q-residual analysis serves as effective proxy for epistemic uncertainty in larger simulations.
AI.conclusion: uMLIP bias significantly impacts fine-tuning outcomes; periodic fine-tuning with multiple steps is essential for generalizable models. Principal component analysis and Q-residual metrics provide valuable tools for identifying unphysical behavior and quantifying uncertainty in molecular dynamics simulations.

title: Persistent short-range charge correlations revealed by ultrafast melting of electronic order in YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6+x}$
summary: Charge density waves (CDW) are ubiquitous in the complex phase diagram of cuprate superconductors and exhibit both short- and long-range correlations. Using time-resolved resonant X-ray scattering, we investigate the photo-induced dynamics of CDW in YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.67}$. We discover an excitation threshold ($Φ$$_\mathrm{C}$ $\approx$ 65 $μ$J/cm$^2$) above which long-range CDW disappear, revealing a persistent CDW peak with short-range correlation length. Ultrafast photo-excitation promptly uncovers this residual short-range CDW correlations, appearing within $\approx$ 0.2 ps. Long-range CDW coherence recovers within $\approx$ 0.6 ps, while the peak intensity remains partially suppressed. We rationalize the dichotomic behavior in the fluence and temporal dependencies as the signature of two coexisting CDW peaks, arising from short- and long-range correlations, which we disentangle through their distinct response to photo-excitation. We provide evidence that the collapse of long-range correlations is driven by an electronic process, while short-range correlations are characterized by distinct timescales and stiffness against photo-excitation. This approach establishes ultrafast X-ray scattering as an effective tool for disentangling coexisting density waves and correlations in quantum materials.

AI.tldr: Time-resolved X-ray scattering reveals two coexisting charge density waves (CDW) in YBa2Cu3O6.67: short-range correlations that persist above a photo-excitation threshold and long-range correlations that collapse above this threshold but recover quickly.
AI.motivation: To understand the complex phase diagram of cuprate superconductors where CDWs exhibit both short- and long-range correlations, and to develop methods for disentangling coexisting density waves in quantum materials.
AI.method: Time-resolved resonant X-ray scattering on YBa2Cu3O6.67 with ultrafast photo-excitation, measuring CDW dynamics across different fluence regimes and temporal scales.
AI.result: Discovered excitation threshold (ΦC ≈ 65 μJ/cm²) above which long-range CDW disappears while short-range CDW persists. Short-range correlations appear within ≈0.2 ps, long-range coherence recovers within ≈0.6 ps, with distinct electronic and structural response characteristics.
AI.conclusion: Two coexisting CDW peaks with different correlation lengths respond distinctly to photo-excitation, with long-range correlations driven by electronic processes and short-range correlations showing different timescales and stiffness, establishing ultrafast X-ray scattering as a tool for disentangling coexisting correlations.

title: Symmetric localization of $ν_{\text{tot}}=4/3$ fractional topological insulator edges
summary: Motivated by the recent twisted MoTe$_2$ experiment [arXiv:2601.18508], we develop a disordered interacting edge theory of a fractional topological insulator at $ν_{\text{tot}}=4/3$, consisting of two time-reversal-conjugated $ν=2/3$ fractional quantum Hall states. For an $S_z$-conserving edge, we uncover three distinct phases with two possible conductance values per edge in the long-edge limit: $\frac{2}{3}\frac{e^2}{h}$ and $\frac{4}{3}\frac{e^2}{h}$. In the presence of $S_z$-changing perturbations (e.g., Rashba spin-orbit coupling), an interaction-induced insulating edge state can emerge without breaking time-reversal or charge-conservation symmetry, corresponding to the absence of a topologically protected edge state. We further provide an exact mapping to a noninteracting fermionic theory exhibiting Anderson localization. Our results showcase an explicit, experimentally relevant example that the edge-state two-terminal transport is insufficient to identify the $ν_{\text{tot}}=4/3$ fractional topological insulators.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a disordered interacting edge theory for a ν_tot=4/3 fractional topological insulator, revealing multiple conductance phases and an interaction-induced insulating edge state that challenges conventional edge transport identification methods.
AI.motivation: Motivated by recent twisted MoTe2 experiments, the study aims to understand the edge physics of fractional topological insulators at ν_tot=4/3, particularly how disorder and interactions affect edge transport and the identification of topological phases.
AI.method: Developed a disordered interacting edge theory for a fractional topological insulator consisting of two time-reversal-conjugated ν=2/3 fractional quantum Hall states. Analyzed both Sz-conserving and Sz-changing perturbations, and provided an exact mapping to a noninteracting fermionic theory exhibiting Anderson localization.
AI.result: For Sz-conserving edges, found three distinct phases with two possible conductance values: 2/3 e²/h and 4/3 e²/h. With Sz-changing perturbations, discovered an interaction-induced insulating edge state emerges without breaking time-reversal or charge-conservation symmetry. Established that two-terminal transport alone is insufficient to identify ν_tot=4/3 fractional topological insulators.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that edge transport measurements in fractional topological insulators can be misleading due to interaction-induced insulating states, highlighting the need for more comprehensive characterization methods beyond simple conductance measurements.

title: Engineering photomagnetism in collinear van der Waals antiferromagnets
summary: Achieving efficient ultrafast optical control of antiferromagnetic spin dynamics is a central goal for next-generation high-speed THz spintronic and magnonic devices. Resonant optical pumping of crystal-field-split d-d orbital multiplets in magnetic TM ions directly modulates exchange and spin-orbit interactions, inducing large-amplitude coherent spin precession. However, such effects are limited to a handful of systems and there is no general strategy to enhance d-d photomagnetism in antiferromagnets. Here, we demonstrate the engineering of photomagnetism via TM-ion doping in collinear van der Waals antiferromagnets. In Mn$_{1-x}$Ni$_x$PS$_3$, small amounts of Ni$^{2+}$ activate a strong photomagnetic response while largely preserving the Néel ground state. Even 10% Ni boosts the response by more than an order of magnitude compared to pure MnPS$_3$, with resonant pumping of Ni$^{2+}$ d-d transitions driving large-amplitude coherent spin precession and providing helicity-dependent phase control. Tuning the pump energy across the full Mn$_{1-x}$Ni$_x$PS$_3$ composition range shows that Ni excitations remain effective across competing Néel and zig-zag antiferromagnetic states while supporting tunable-frequency coherent spin precession. These results establish TM-ion doping as a versatile strategy to harness orbital multiplet excitations for ultrafast, low-dissipation spin control in van der Waals antiferromagnets.

AI.tldr: Transition metal ion doping in van der Waals antiferromagnets enables strong photomagnetic response and coherent spin precession via resonant pumping of d-d orbital transitions.
AI.motivation: Achieving efficient ultrafast optical control of antiferromagnetic spin dynamics is crucial for next-generation high-speed THz spintronic and magnonic devices, but current approaches are limited to few systems with no general enhancement strategy.
AI.method: Engineering photomagnetism via transition metal ion doping in collinear van der Waals antiferromagnets (Mn$_{1-x}$Ni$_x$PS$_3$), where Ni$^{2+}$ doping activates strong photomagnetic response while preserving Néel ground state.
AI.result: 10% Ni doping boosts photomagnetic response by more than an order of magnitude compared to pure MnPS$_3$, with resonant pumping of Ni$^{2+}$ d-d transitions driving large-amplitude coherent spin precession and providing helicity-dependent phase control.
AI.conclusion: Transition metal ion doping establishes a versatile strategy to harness orbital multiplet excitations for ultrafast, low-dissipation spin control in van der Waals antiferromagnets, working across competing magnetic states while supporting tunable-frequency coherent spin precession.

title: Pauli-limited upper critical field and anisotropic depairing effect of La2.82Sr0.18Ni2O7 superconducting thin film
summary: We investigate the upper critical field and superconducting anisotropy of epitaxial La2.82Sr0.18Ni2O7 thin films, which show a sharp superconducting transition at Tc=31.6 K. Near Tc, superconductivity exhibits thickness-limited two-dimensional characteristics. Upon cooling, the out-of-plane coherence length decreases below the sample thickness of 6 nm, corresponding to a 3-unit-cell film, indicating a crossover to intrinsic three-dimensional bulk superconductivity. High-field transport measurements reveal large upper critical fields with a small anisotropy ratio gama~1.34, comparable to bulk Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates. At low temperatures, the in-plane (ab) upper critical field Hc2(ab) is strongly suppressed by spin-paramagnetic pair breaking and approaches the Pauli limit (Hc2(Pauli)=58 T), while Hc2(c) remains largely unaffected. This anisotropic Pauli limitation accounts for the reduced upper critical field anisotropy and supports the conclusion that superconductivity in these films is fundamentally three-dimensional bulk like. Our results highlight the essential role of spin-paramagnetic effects in shaping the high-field superconducting phase diagram of Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates.

AI.tldr: La2.82Sr0.18Ni2O7 thin films show 3D bulk superconductivity with small anisotropy (γ~1.34), where spin-paramagnetic pair breaking suppresses in-plane upper critical field near Pauli limit, revealing essential role of spin effects in nickelate superconductivity.
AI.motivation: To investigate the dimensionality crossover and upper critical field behavior in epitaxial La2.82Sr0.18Ni2O7 thin films, particularly understanding how spin-paramagnetic effects influence the superconducting phase diagram in Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates.
AI.method: Studied epitaxial La2.82Sr0.18Ni2O7 thin films with Tc=31.6 K using high-field transport measurements to determine upper critical fields Hc2(ab) and Hc2(c), analyzed coherence length evolution with temperature, and examined thickness-dependent dimensionality crossover from 2D to 3D behavior.
AI.result: Films show thickness-limited 2D superconductivity near Tc but crossover to intrinsic 3D bulk superconductivity upon cooling. Small anisotropy ratio γ~1.34 comparable to bulk nickelates. Hc2(ab) strongly suppressed by spin-paramagnetic pair breaking approaching Pauli limit (58 T), while Hc2(c) unaffected, leading to reduced anisotropy and confirming 3D bulk-like superconductivity.
AI.conclusion: Superconductivity in La2.82Sr0.18Ni2O7 thin films is fundamentally three-dimensional bulk-like with small anisotropy. Spin-paramagnetic pair breaking plays essential role in shaping high-field superconducting phase diagram of Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates, particularly suppressing in-plane upper critical field near Pauli limit.

title: Classical Kitaev model in a magnetic field
summary: Motivated by experiments on spin-orbit coupled magnets with Kitaev exchange in magnetic fields, we present an analysis of the classical Kitaev honeycomb model in the presence of a magnetic field. We show that there is a spin liquid regime that exists within a finite window of fields from zero up to a finite threshold before transitioning into the polarized paramagnet. We uncover constraints that spins need to satisfy in the ground state and show that they determine the exact limiting zero temperature behavior of the heat capacity and magnetic susceptibility within the spin liquid as a function of field. When the field is finite, both the two-point spin and the quadrupolar correlations are short-ranged, in contrast to the zero-field case. We rationalize an effective mass for the quadrupolar correlations in terms of a coarse-grained theory with fluctuating effective charge degrees of freedom. Finally, we show that weak site-dilution does not change the magnetization within the spin liquid -- a kind of "perfect" compensation of the site dilution.

AI.tldr: Classical Kitaev honeycomb model in magnetic field shows spin liquid regime from zero to finite field threshold, with exact zero-temperature heat capacity/susceptibility behavior, short-range correlations, and perfect compensation against site dilution.
AI.motivation: Motivated by experiments on spin-orbit coupled magnets with Kitaev exchange in magnetic fields, to understand the classical Kitaev honeycomb model under applied magnetic fields.
AI.method: Analysis of classical Kitaev honeycomb model with magnetic field, uncovering ground state constraints, calculating zero-temperature behavior of heat capacity and susceptibility, studying spin and quadrupolar correlations, developing coarse-grained theory with fluctuating effective charges, and examining effects of weak site-dilution.
AI.result: Spin liquid regime exists within finite field window (zero to threshold) before transitioning to polarized paramagnet; exact zero-temperature behavior of heat capacity and susceptibility determined by ground state constraints; finite field yields short-range spin and quadrupolar correlations (unlike zero-field case); effective mass for quadrupolar correlations rationalized via coarse-grained theory; weak site-dilution does not affect magnetization in spin liquid (perfect compensation).
AI.conclusion: Classical Kitaev model in magnetic field hosts robust spin liquid phase with well-defined thermodynamic properties, short-range correlations, and remarkable stability against site dilution due to perfect compensation mechanism.

title: Flexible Cutoff Learning: Optimizing Machine Learning Potentials After Training
summary: We introduce Flexible Cutoff Learning (FCL), a method for training machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) whose cutoff radii can be adjusted after training. Unlike conventional MLIPs that fix the cutoff radius during training, FCL models are trained by randomly sampling cutoff radii independently for each atom. The resulting model can then be deployed with different per-atom cutoff radii depending on the application, enabling application-specific optimization of the accuracy-cost tradeoff. Using a differentiable cost model, these per-atom cutoffs can be optimized for specific target systems after training. We demonstrate FCL with a modified MACE architecture trained on the MAD dataset. For a subset featuring molecular crystals, optimized per-atom cutoffs reduce computational cost by more than 60% while increasing force errors by less than 1%. These results show that FCL enables training of a single general-purpose MLIP that can be adapted to diverse applications through post-training cutoff optimization, eliminating the need for retraining.

AI.tldr: FCL enables MLIPs with adjustable cutoff radii after training, allowing application-specific optimization of accuracy-cost tradeoffs without retraining.
AI.motivation: Conventional MLIPs fix cutoff radii during training, limiting flexibility for different applications where computational cost vs. accuracy tradeoffs vary. There's a need for general-purpose potentials that can be adapted post-training to specific use cases.
AI.method: Train MLIPs by randomly sampling cutoff radii independently for each atom during training. Use a differentiable cost model to optimize per-atom cutoffs for specific target systems after training. Implemented with modified MACE architecture on MAD dataset.
AI.result: For molecular crystal subset, optimized per-atom cutoffs reduce computational cost by >60% while increasing force errors by <1%. Enables single general-purpose MLIP adaptable to diverse applications through post-training cutoff optimization.
AI.conclusion: FCL eliminates need for retraining by enabling training of flexible MLIPs whose cutoff radii can be adjusted post-training, allowing application-specific optimization of accuracy-cost tradeoffs.

title: Gap structure and phase diagram of twisted bilayer cuprates from a microscopic perspective
summary: Since the prediction of a time-reversal symmetry breaking (TRSB) $d+id^\prime$ state in twisted bilayer cuprate superconductors by Can et al. in 2021, several experiments have attempted to detect this state, yielding conflicting results. At present, it is not clear which differences in samples or experimental conditions might explain these discrepancies. In this work, we perform a tight-binding lattice model calculation with phenomenological interlayer tunneling, examining the order parameter as a function of twist angle, interlayer tunneling, doping, and temperature. We observe the TRSB state to be correlated to the position of the Van Hove singularity in the normal state which changes not only as a function of doping but also the tunneling strength. Two such phases are identified as nominally consistent with in-plane $d+id'$ and $d+is$ order, but with unexpected transformation properties under bilayer symmetry operations. We calculate the Josephson critical current, in particular examining the angle dependence for various tunneling strengths. Finally, we discuss the existing experiments in the context of our results.

AI.tldr: TRSB d+id' state in twisted bilayer cuprates shows conflicting experimental results; theoretical study reveals correlation with Van Hove singularity position, identifies two TRSB phases with unusual symmetry properties, calculates Josephson critical current, and discusses experimental discrepancies.
AI.motivation: Resolve conflicting experimental results on time-reversal symmetry breaking d+id' state in twisted bilayer cuprate superconductors by understanding how sample differences and experimental conditions affect the state's stability and properties.
AI.method: Tight-binding lattice model calculation with phenomenological interlayer tunneling, examining order parameter as function of twist angle, interlayer tunneling, doping, and temperature; calculation of Josephson critical current with angle dependence analysis.
AI.result: TRSB state correlates with Van Hove singularity position in normal state (dependent on doping and tunneling strength); identifies two TRSB phases nominally consistent with d+id' and d+is order but with unexpected bilayer symmetry transformation properties; calculates Josephson critical current angle dependence.
AI.conclusion: Theoretical framework explains experimental discrepancies by linking TRSB state stability to Van Hove singularity position, identifies unconventional symmetry properties of TRSB phases, and provides Josephson current predictions for experimental comparison.

title: Disorder-induced localisation in the Mott-Hubbard model
summary: For the Fermi-Hubbard model in the Mott insulator phase, we employ the hierarchy of correlations to study how doublon and holon quasi-particle excitations are affected by adding disorder to the system. We study two types of disorder: charge disorder, in the form of on-site potential randomness; and spin disorder, in the form of a fixed, randomly generated background spin arrangement. By analysing the quasi-particle eigen-spectra and quantifying the degree to which the corresponding eigen-states localise, we find both an energetic and spatial separation between localised and delocalised states in the charge disorder. In contrast, the spin disorder results in localised states throughout the quasi-particle bands. Finally, we repeat our calculations using strong-coupling perturbation theory, and compare the results obtained from both methods.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how disorder affects doublon and holon excitations in the Mott insulator phase of the Fermi-Hubbard model using hierarchy of correlations and strong-coupling perturbation theory, comparing charge disorder (on-site potential randomness) and spin disorder (random background spin arrangement).
AI.motivation: To understand how different types of disorder (charge and spin) affect the localization properties of quasi-particle excitations (doublons and holons) in the Mott insulator phase of the Fermi-Hubbard model, and to compare results from hierarchy of correlations with strong-coupling perturbation theory.
AI.method: Employed hierarchy of correlations to study doublon and holon quasi-particle excitations under disorder; analyzed quasi-particle eigen-spectra and quantified eigen-state localization; studied two disorder types: charge disorder (on-site potential randomness) and spin disorder (fixed random background spin arrangement); compared with strong-coupling perturbation theory calculations.
AI.result: Charge disorder produces both energetic and spatial separation between localized and delocalized states, while spin disorder results in localized states throughout the quasi-particle bands. Comparison between hierarchy of correlations and strong-coupling perturbation theory shows consistent findings.
AI.conclusion: Different types of disorder have distinct effects on quasi-particle localization in Mott insulators: charge disorder creates a mobility edge separating localized and delocalized states, while spin disorder leads to complete localization across the bands. Both theoretical methods yield consistent results.

title: Structural and Optical Characteristics of beta-Ga2O3 Implanted with Rare Earth Ions
summary:
We investigated the structural evolution and optical properties of beta-Ga2O3 crystals implanted with different rare-earth (RE) ions using channeling Rutherford Backscattering Spectrometry, Positron Annihilation, Photoluminescence, and Photoluminescence Excitation spectroscopies. The studies reveal that implantation-induced disorder, accompanying phase transitions, and post-annealing structural recovery are largely insensitive to the implanted RE species. The defect microstructure is also found to be similar for all implanted RE ions.
  Thermal annealing does not completely remove radiation-induced defects but instead drives their rearrangement into larger defect complexes. Unimplanted (virgin) beta-Ga2O3 exhibits strong UV-visible emission attributed to oxygen vacancies, whereas the introduction of RE ions produces additional emission lines originating from electronic transitions within RE3+ ions.
  The results indicate that RE3+ ions are excited through the host conduction band, followed by non-radiative relaxation to the 4f excited states and radiative decay to the respective ground states. Fluence-dependent studies of Yb3+ reveal the onset of concentration quenching, while RE-related emission remains efficient even in the presence of substantial lattice disorder.
  These findings provide new insight into defect evolution in ion-implanted beta-Ga2O3 and clarify the excitation mechanisms of RE3+ ions, offering guidance for optimizing the optical performance of beta-Ga2O3:RE materials.

AI.tldr: Rare-earth ion implantation in beta-Ga2O3 shows similar structural damage and defect evolution regardless of RE species, with RE³⁺ ions excited via host conduction band and emitting efficiently even with lattice disorder.
AI.motivation: To understand how different rare-earth ions affect structural evolution and optical properties in ion-implanted beta-Ga2O3 crystals, and to clarify the excitation mechanisms of RE³⁺ ions in this host material.
AI.method: Used channeling Rutherford Backscattering Spectrometry, Positron Annihilation, Photoluminescence, and Photoluminescence Excitation spectroscopies to study beta-Ga2O3 crystals implanted with various RE ions, examining structural changes and optical properties.
AI.result: Implantation-induced disorder, phase transitions, and post-annealing recovery are insensitive to RE species. Thermal annealing rearranges defects into larger complexes rather than removing them. RE³⁺ ions are excited through host conduction band, followed by non-radiative relaxation to 4f excited states and radiative decay. Yb³⁺ shows concentration quenching, but RE-related emission remains efficient despite lattice disorder.
AI.conclusion: The study provides new insights into defect evolution in ion-implanted beta-Ga2O3 and clarifies RE³⁺ excitation mechanisms, offering guidance for optimizing optical performance of beta-Ga2O3:RE materials for potential optoelectronic applications.

title: Supercurrents in Josephson junctions with chiral molecular potentials
summary: The influence of chiral molecular potentials on phase-coherent transport in superconducting Josephson junctions is investigated. Within a Bogoliubov-de Gennes tight-binding framework, an SNS junction functionalized by adsorbed chiral molecules is modeled, where electrostatic gradients generated by the molecules induce spin-orbit coupling in the normal region. The equilibrium charge current-phase relation is found to remain largely insensitive to molecular chirality in symmetric, zero-field configurations. In contrast, the spin supercurrent exhibits a pronounced chirality-dependent response, with opposite enantiomers producing distinct and anisotropic spin-polarized Josephson currents. The resulting handedness contrast can be enhanced through control parameters such as molecular orientation and the strength of the induced spin-orbit coupling. The temperature dependence of these currents further shows that the chirality-dependent signatures persist across a range of temperatures well below the superconducting critical temperature. These results establish Josephson interferometry as a phase-sensitive and accessible platform for detecting molecular chirality and highlight spin-polarized superconducting transport as a promising route toward integrating chiral molecular functionality into superconducting spintronic devices.

AI.tldr: Chiral molecules in superconducting Josephson junctions induce spin-orbit coupling, creating chirality-dependent spin supercurrents but not affecting equilibrium charge currents in symmetric configurations.
AI.motivation: To investigate how chiral molecular potentials influence phase-coherent transport in superconducting Josephson junctions and explore the integration of chiral molecular functionality into superconducting spintronic devices.
AI.method: Using a Bogoliubov-de Gennes tight-binding framework to model an SNS junction functionalized by adsorbed chiral molecules, where electrostatic gradients from the molecules induce spin-orbit coupling in the normal region.
AI.result: Equilibrium charge current-phase relation remains insensitive to molecular chirality in symmetric, zero-field configurations, while spin supercurrent shows pronounced chirality-dependent response with opposite enantiomers producing distinct anisotropic spin-polarized Josephson currents. Chirality contrast can be enhanced via molecular orientation and spin-orbit coupling strength, with signatures persisting across temperatures well below superconducting critical temperature.
AI.conclusion: Josephson interferometry serves as a phase-sensitive platform for detecting molecular chirality, and spin-polarized superconducting transport offers a promising route for integrating chiral molecular functionality into superconducting spintronic devices.

title: Long-range magnetic order with disordered spin orientations in a high-entropy antiferromagnet
comment: 10 pages, plus references, 1 table, 4 figures, and Supplementary information, accepted for publication in Nature Communications
summary: Disorder in magnetic systems typically suppresses long-range order, promoting short-range states such as spin glasses and magnetic clusters. This is particularly prominent in high-entropy materials, characterized by the random distributions of local magnetic entities and exchange interactions. However, in rare exceptions, long-range magnetic order can persist in high-entropy systems, while the microscopic characters and underlying mechanisms remain elusive, especially the magnetic behaviors of individual elements. Here, combining neutron diffraction and resonant soft x-ray scattering, we have conducted an element-specific investigation into the magnetic order of a high-entropy honeycomb-lattice van der Waals material (Mn1/4Fe1/4Co1/4Ni1/4)PS3. Despite significant atomic disorder, long-range zigzag antiferromagnetic order is observed below 72 K, with all four transition-metal elements participating in a unified phase transition. However, the spin orientations of various elements are distinct, attributed to the competition between single-ion anisotropies and exchange interactions. Our findings showcase a novel form of long-range magnetic order with disordered spin orientations, which is synergically stabilized by distinct magnetic elements in a high entropy magnet, offering a new paradigm for understanding complex magnetic systems.

AI.tldr: High-entropy honeycomb van der Waals material (Mn1/4Fe1/4Co1/4Ni1/4)PS3 exhibits long-range zigzag antiferromagnetic order despite atomic disorder, with all four transition metals participating in a unified phase transition but with distinct spin orientations.
AI.motivation: To understand how long-range magnetic order can persist in high-entropy systems despite atomic disorder, and to investigate the microscopic magnetic behaviors of individual elements in such complex magnetic systems.
AI.method: Combined neutron diffraction and resonant soft x-ray scattering for element-specific investigation of magnetic order in high-entropy honeycomb-lattice van der Waals material (Mn1/4Fe1/4Co1/4Ni1/4)PS3.
AI.result: Long-range zigzag antiferromagnetic order observed below 72 K with all four transition-metal elements participating in a unified phase transition. However, spin orientations of various elements are distinct due to competition between single-ion anisotropies and exchange interactions.
AI.conclusion: Discovery of a novel form of long-range magnetic order with disordered spin orientations, synergically stabilized by distinct magnetic elements in a high-entropy magnet, offering a new paradigm for understanding complex magnetic systems.

title: A fully solution-processed organic microcavity laser in the strong light-matter coupling regime
summary: Solid-state semiconductor lasers underpin technologies from telecommunications and data storage to sensing, medical diagnostics, and emerging quantum communication. Polaritons-hybrid exciton-photon states have further extended this reach, enabling room-temperature quantum effects such as low-threshold lasing and single-photon nonlinearities. Organic semiconductors are ideal for polaritonics due to their large exciton binding energy, strong optical nonlinearities, and straightforward processing, making them attractive for both classical and quantum photonics. While solution-processed organic films have been widely explored, their optical cavities have almost always been fabricated using vacuum deposition, limiting the realization of truly scalable and low-cost devices. Here, we report the first organic laser microcavities fabricated entirely by solution processing, which operate in the strong coupling regimeThe resulting platform can be driven reliably to high excitation densities, where we observe a reversible, interaction-driven redistribution of the polariton condensate, revealing a distinct polariton lasing behaviour in organic microcavities. Together, the fabrication approach and the observed lasing dynamics establish a route toward scalable polaritonic and quantum photonic technologies and provide new opportunities for studying nonlinear polariton physics in organic systems.

AI.tldr: First demonstration of fully solution-processed organic polariton microcavities operating in strong coupling regime, showing reversible polariton condensation and lasing behavior.
AI.motivation: Organic semiconductors offer advantages for polaritonics (large exciton binding energy, strong nonlinearities, easy processing) but current fabrication relies on vacuum deposition, limiting scalability and cost-effectiveness. Need for fully solution-processed organic polariton devices.
AI.method: Fabricated organic laser microcavities entirely by solution processing techniques (no vacuum deposition). Demonstrated operation in strong coupling regime and studied polariton behavior under high excitation densities.
AI.result: Successfully created solution-processed organic microcavities operating in strong coupling regime. Observed reversible, interaction-driven redistribution of polariton condensate under high excitation, revealing distinct polariton lasing behavior in organic systems.
AI.conclusion: The fabrication approach enables scalable, low-cost polaritonic and quantum photonic technologies, while the observed lasing dynamics opens new opportunities for studying nonlinear polariton physics in organic systems.

title: Ab-initio superfluid weight and superconducting penetration depth
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to Physical Review B as a regular article on the 2nd of March 2026
summary:
Machine learning and high-throughput screening approaches to superconductor discovery require physically meaningful descriptors that capture essential physics while remaining computationally tractable. The superfluid weight is an ideal descriptor as it is a prerequisite for superconductivity, determines the magnetic penetration depth and the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition temperature in two-dimensional materials, may limit the critical temperature in unconventional superconductors through phase coherence, and reveals quantum geometric contributions to supercurrent transport. We develop a computationally efficient framework for calculating the zero-temperature, mean-field superfluid weight for uniform pairing from density functional theory band structures and Bloch wavefunctions. We separately evaluate the conventional contribution from band curvature and the geometric contribution from quantum geometry. To validate the method, we calculate London penetration depths for a few conventional superconductors (Al, Pb, Nb, MgB$_2$, LuRu$_3$B$_2$ and YRu$_3$B$_2$) and find good agreement with experiment after accounting for nonlocal corrections, strong-coupling effects, and sample quality.
  The conventional contribution dominates by orders of magnitude in these wide-band materials, as expected. This framework provides a foundation for large-scale screening of superconducting candidates and exploring quantum geometric effects in unconventional superconductors.

AI.tldr: A computational framework for efficient calculation of superfluid weight from DFT band structures, separating conventional and quantum geometric contributions, validated on conventional superconductors.
AI.motivation: Machine learning and high-throughput screening for superconductor discovery require physically meaningful yet computationally efficient descriptors. Superfluid weight is ideal as it captures essential physics of superconductivity, determines key properties like magnetic penetration depth and transition temperatures, and reveals quantum geometric contributions to supercurrent transport.
AI.method: Developed a computationally efficient framework for calculating zero-temperature, mean-field superfluid weight for uniform pairing from density functional theory (DFT) band structures and Bloch wavefunctions. The method separately evaluates conventional contribution from band curvature and geometric contribution from quantum geometry.
AI.result: Validated the method by calculating London penetration depths for conventional superconductors (Al, Pb, Nb, MgB₂, LuRu₃B₂, YRu₃B₂), finding good agreement with experiment after accounting for nonlocal corrections, strong-coupling effects, and sample quality. Conventional contribution dominates by orders of magnitude in wide-band materials as expected.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a foundation for large-scale screening of superconducting candidates and exploring quantum geometric effects in unconventional superconductors, enabling efficient computational discovery and analysis of superconducting materials.

title: Ab initio quantum embedding description of magic angle twisted bilayer graphene at even-integer fillings
summary: Magic angle twisted bilayer graphene (MATBG) hosts narrow moiré bands with meV-scale energy splittings, making its correlated phases sensitive to both material parameters and modeling choices in low-energy downfolding. We develop an ab initio quantum-embedding workflow that derives interacting flat-band Hamiltonians from Kohn-Sham density functional theory (KS-DFT) of a relaxed, unstrained structure. Our model combines constrained random phase approximation (cRPA) screening, controlled double-counting subtraction, and an automated gauge-fixing procedure based on the selected columns of the density matrix (SCDM) that is compatible with symmetry-resolved many-body calculations. Solving the resulting models using Hartree-Fock (HF) and coupled cluster singles and doubles (CCSD), we recover robust insulating Kramers intervalley coherent (KIVC) states at charge neutrality ($ν=0$) and at electron doping ($ν=+2$). The main new physical effect appears on the hole-doped side: at $ν=-2$ we observe a fragile semimetal with a weak $\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}$ Kekulé modulation and enhanced intervalley-scattering peaks in the Fourier-transformed local density of states. Although the underlying KS-DFT band structure is nearly particle-hole symmetric, the effective interacting Hamiltonian exhibits a pronounced particle-hole asymmetry at $ν=\pm 2$ that we trace to momentum-dependent single-particle renormalizations generated by subtraction terms constructed from reference densities consistent with the KS-DFT filling. Our work provides a first-principles route for connecting microscopic electronic structure, screened interactions, subtraction choices, and scanning tunneling microscopy signatures in MATBG.

AI.tldr: Ab initio quantum-embedding workflow derives interacting flat-band Hamiltonians for magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, revealing robust KIVC insulators at ν=0 and +2, and a fragile semimetal with Kekulé modulation at ν=-2, with pronounced particle-hole asymmetry traced to momentum-dependent renormalizations.
AI.motivation: MATBG's narrow moiré bands with meV-scale splittings make correlated phases sensitive to material parameters and modeling choices, requiring a first-principles approach to connect microscopic electronic structure, screened interactions, and experimental signatures.
AI.method: Ab initio quantum-embedding workflow combining: (1) Kohn-Sham DFT of relaxed, unstrained structure; (2) constrained RPA screening; (3) controlled double-counting subtraction; (4) automated gauge-fixing via SCDM compatible with symmetry-resolved many-body calculations; (5) solving models with Hartree-Fock and CCSD.
AI.result: Recover robust insulating Kramers intervalley coherent (KIVC) states at ν=0 and ν=+2; at ν=-2 observe fragile semimetal with weak √3×√3 Kekulé modulation and enhanced intervalley-scattering peaks in FT-LDOS; pronounced particle-hole asymmetry at ν=±2 traced to momentum-dependent single-particle renormalizations from subtraction terms.
AI.conclusion: Provides first-principles route connecting microscopic electronic structure, screened interactions, subtraction choices, and STM signatures in MATBG, revealing how particle-hole asymmetry emerges despite nearly symmetric KS-DFT band structure through momentum-dependent renormalizations.

title: Frontiers of atom probe tomography physics, data processing, and analysis
comment: 43 pages, 7 multicomponent figures, summary of workshop
summary: Atom probe tomography (APT) fills a crucial need in the characterization workflow of materials by its ability to inform the 3D chemical microstructure at the nanoscale. As with any characterization techniques, APT has strengths and limitations that inform the interpretation of the data. Therefore, a challenge for the materials characterization community, and the APT community in particular, is the need to establish repeatable and reproducible workflows around the APT data acquisition, reconstruction, analysis, and sharing, in order to inform interpretation. Data interpretation also requires the continued development of our understanding of the physical processes responsible for field evaporation. We review recent developments in the experimental analysis of field evaporation and in the modeling of field evaporation leading to new understanding of common artifacts observed in reconstructed data. We then discuss current challenges with data analysis, translation of results, and data interpretation in the absence of community-agreed standards, and therefore, the crucial need for standardization at every stage of APT research, from data collection all the way to data reporting. This perspective is a summary of the invited presentations and discussions that took place during a workshop (August 4-5, 2024, Alexandria, Virginia, USA).

AI.tldr: This perspective paper reviews challenges in atom probe tomography (APT) data interpretation, emphasizing the need for standardized workflows from data acquisition to reporting to ensure reproducibility and reliable materials characterization.
AI.motivation: APT provides crucial 3D chemical microstructure data at nanoscale, but interpretation is challenged by technique limitations, artifacts, and lack of community standards, necessitating reproducible workflows and better understanding of field evaporation physics.
AI.method: The paper reviews recent developments in experimental analysis and modeling of field evaporation processes, discusses current data analysis challenges, and synthesizes insights from a workshop with invited presentations and discussions.
AI.result: The review identifies common artifacts in APT reconstructions linked to field evaporation processes, highlights challenges in data analysis and interpretation without community standards, and emphasizes the need for standardization at all research stages.
AI.conclusion: Standardization is crucial throughout APT research - from data collection to reporting - to establish reproducible workflows, improve data interpretation, and advance materials characterization capabilities through community-agreed standards.

title: Observation of Kondo hybridization wave in UTe2
summary: Condensed matter systems with strong electronic correlations often manifest a variety of intertwined ordered phases of charge, spin, orbital and other degrees of freedom. As a prototypical strongly correlated electronic system, the Kondo lattice provides fertile soil for many fascinating quantum states, including quantum criticality, unconventional superconductivity, hidden order and topological Kondo insulator/semimetal. The foundation of Kondo physics lies in the hybridization between localized moments and itinerant electrons. Generally, the evolution of Kondo hybridization is characterized as a broad crossover rather than a phase transition. Thus far, an ordered hybridization phase has not been observed. Here, we use scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) to identify a translational-symmetry-breaking order of Kondo hybridization wave(KHW) for the first time on the surface of the spin-triplet heavy-fermion superconductor UTe2. The unprecedented phase of KHW manifests as a periodically modulated Fano lattice, accompanied by a commensurate charge density wave (CDW) and a pronounced energy gap opening near the Fermi level. This KHW-imprinted CDW has an intriguing real-space texture of complementary occupation of the heavy f and conduction charges, thereby forming a Kondo superlattice. The KHW is coexistent with superconductivity in UTe2, which may provide valuable insight into its controversial spin-triplet pairing symmetry and the underlying mechanism. Our first experimental evidence for an ordered hybridization state potentially sheds new light on the strong correlation physics of Kondo lattice system.

AI.tldr: First experimental observation of an ordered Kondo hybridization wave (KHW) phase in UTe2, manifested as a periodically modulated Fano lattice with a commensurate charge density wave and energy gap near Fermi level.
AI.motivation: To investigate the fundamental question of whether Kondo hybridization can form an ordered phase, as previous understanding characterized it as a broad crossover rather than a phase transition, and to explore new quantum states in strongly correlated systems.
AI.method: Used scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) to study the surface of spin-triplet heavy-fermion superconductor UTe2, identifying translational-symmetry-breaking order of Kondo hybridization wave through analysis of Fano lattice patterns and charge density wave formation.
AI.result: Discovered the first ordered hybridization phase in a Kondo lattice system, characterized by: (1) periodically modulated Fano lattice, (2) commensurate charge density wave, (3) energy gap opening near Fermi level, (4) complementary occupation of heavy f and conduction charges forming a Kondo superlattice, and (5) coexistence with superconductivity.
AI.conclusion: This represents the first experimental evidence for an ordered hybridization state in Kondo lattice systems, potentially providing new insights into strong correlation physics and the controversial spin-triplet pairing symmetry in UTe2.

title: Electron-phonon physics at the exascale: A hybrid MPI-GPU-OpenMP framework for scalable Wannier interpolation
comment: 30 pages, 13 figures; accepted in npj Computational Materials
summary: We demonstrate a highly efficient GPU implementation of the Wannier interpolation of electron-phonon matrix elements in the EPW code. Building on a systematic analysis of the computational complexity of the algorithm for electron-phonon interpolation, we designed a GPU porting strategy that integrates naturally into the current EPW implementation, and is seamlessly portable to NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs. We demonstrate this development via extensive benchmarks on conventional semiconductors such as silicon and monolayer MoS$_2$, as well as a large-scale application to topological stanene nanoribbons of width as large as 20nm, which was intractable with previous implementations. Compared to the single MPI parallelization scheme of EPW v5.9, the resulting hybrid MPI-GPU-OpenMP scheme achieves up to 29-fold speedup on leadership-class supercomputers equipped with NVIDIA and Intel accelerators, namely Vista at the Texas Advanced Computing Center, Perlmutter at the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center, and Aurora at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility. This framework also achieves nearly ideal scalability up to thousands of GPU nodes on the Aurora supercomputer. With this development, EPW is ready to support electron-phonon physics calculations on exascale platforms.

AI.tldr: GPU-accelerated implementation of Wannier interpolation for electron-phonon matrix elements in EPW code achieves up to 29× speedup and scales to thousands of GPU nodes on exascale platforms.
AI.motivation: Previous EPW implementations were limited in scalability and computational efficiency, making large-scale electron-phonon calculations (like 20nm topological stanene nanoribbons) intractable. There was a need for GPU acceleration to enable exascale electron-phonon physics calculations.
AI.method: Systematic analysis of computational complexity of electron-phonon interpolation algorithm, followed by design of GPU porting strategy that integrates into existing EPW implementation. The approach uses hybrid MPI-GPU-OpenMP parallelization and is portable across NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs.
AI.result: Achieved up to 29-fold speedup compared to single MPI parallelization in EPW v5.9. Demonstrated scalability to thousands of GPU nodes on Aurora supercomputer. Enabled previously intractable calculations of 20nm topological stanene nanoribbons. Validated on conventional semiconductors (silicon, monolayer MoS₂) and large-scale systems.
AI.conclusion: The GPU-accelerated EPW implementation enables efficient electron-phonon physics calculations on exascale platforms, overcoming previous computational limitations and opening new possibilities for large-scale materials simulations.

title: Pairing and charge distribution in Emery ladders preserving the ratio of Cu to O atoms
summary: We study the Emery model (three-band Hubbard model) for superconducting cuprates on three distinct ladder-like lattices that are supercell of the CuO$_2$ plane and thus preserve the ratio of copper to oxygen atoms. Using the density-matrix renormalization group method we confirm that these Emery ladders are charge-transfer insulators for the hole concentration corresponding to undoped cuprates but become Luther-Emery liquids with enhanced pairing correlations upon doping. The preservation of the Cu to O ratio allows us to study the distribution of charges between these atoms in the Luther-Emery phase. We show that these Emery ladders can describe the relations between charge distribution, pairing strength, and interactions that have been observed in the Emery model on two-dimensional clusters and in experiments.

AI.tldr: Emery ladders (three-band Hubbard model) preserve Cu:O ratio, show charge-transfer insulator at half-filling, become Luther-Emery liquids with enhanced pairing upon doping, revealing relationships between charge distribution, pairing strength, and interactions.
AI.motivation: To study the Emery model for superconducting cuprates on ladder-like lattices that preserve the copper-to-oxygen ratio, enabling investigation of charge distribution between Cu and O atoms in the Luther-Emery phase and connecting model predictions with experimental observations.
AI.method: Use density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) method to study the three-band Hubbard (Emery) model on three distinct ladder-like lattices that are supercells of the CuO₂ plane, preserving the Cu:O ratio.
AI.result: Emery ladders are charge-transfer insulators at hole concentration corresponding to undoped cuprates, but become Luther-Emery liquids with enhanced pairing correlations upon doping. The preserved Cu:O ratio allows study of charge distribution between atoms, revealing relationships between charge distribution, pairing strength, and interactions consistent with 2D cluster studies and experiments.
AI.conclusion: Emery ladders provide a controlled framework to study relationships between charge distribution, pairing correlations, and interactions in cuprate superconductors, bridging model predictions with experimental observations while preserving key material-specific features like the Cu:O ratio.

title: Formulation of intrinsic nonlinear thermal conductivity for bosonic systems using quantum kinetic equation
summary: Nonlinear responses in transport phenomena have attracted significant attention because they can arise even when linear responses are forbidden by symmetry, with the quantum geometry of Bloch wave functions playing an essential role. While such effects have been extensively studied in electric transport, similar quantum-geometric mechanisms are also expected to govern nonlinear thermal transport. In particular, thermal responses are crucial in bosonic systems such as magnons and phonons, which are charge-neutral quasiparticles. However, a consistent theoretical description of nonlinear thermal transport remains challenging because of the difficulty in the treatment of energy magnetization in higher-order responses with Luttinger's gravitational potential method. Here, we formulate the intrinsic nonlinear thermal conductivity of bosonic systems using a quantum kinetic equation approach that avoids Luttinger's method and naturally incorporates contributions from energy magnetization. We identify three distinct contributions to the nonlinear thermal conductivity: two expressed in terms of quantum-geometric quantities, namely the quantum metric and the thermal Berry-connection polarizability (TBCP), and a third determined solely by the band dispersions. Applying our formalism to a specific quantum spin model within linear spin-wave theory, we show that the TBCP term dominates the nonlinear thermal Hall effect in the absence of threefold symmetry. Our results differ quantitatively from those obtained using semiclassical theory, thereby highlighting the importance of quantum corrections beyond the semiclassical picture. These findings establish a general framework for intrinsic nonlinear thermal responses in bosonic systems and reveal quantum-geometric mechanisms underlying thermal transport beyond linear response theory.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a quantum kinetic theory for intrinsic nonlinear thermal transport in bosonic systems, identifying three contributions including quantum-geometric terms, and shows quantum corrections beyond semiclassical theory.
AI.motivation: Nonlinear responses in transport phenomena have attracted attention due to symmetry-breaking effects and quantum-geometric origins. While extensively studied in electric transport, similar mechanisms should govern nonlinear thermal transport, especially in bosonic systems like magnons and phonons. However, theoretical description remains challenging due to difficulties with energy magnetization in higher-order responses using Luttinger's gravitational potential method.
AI.method: The authors formulate intrinsic nonlinear thermal conductivity using a quantum kinetic equation approach that avoids Luttinger's method and naturally incorporates energy magnetization contributions. They identify three distinct contributions: two expressed in terms of quantum-geometric quantities (quantum metric and thermal Berry-connection polarizability), and a third determined solely by band dispersions.
AI.result: Applying the formalism to a quantum spin model within linear spin-wave theory shows that the thermal Berry-connection polarizability term dominates the nonlinear thermal Hall effect in the absence of threefold symmetry. Results differ quantitatively from semiclassical theory, highlighting the importance of quantum corrections beyond the semiclassical picture.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a general framework for intrinsic nonlinear thermal responses in bosonic systems and reveals quantum-geometric mechanisms underlying thermal transport beyond linear response theory, providing a consistent theoretical description that overcomes previous challenges with energy magnetization treatment.

title: Polarization transfer force on ferroelectric domain walls
summary: We investigate the dynamics of ferroelectric textures driven by polarization currents. We show that, ferrons, the quanta of collective polarization excitations, provide an exotic driving mechanism for domain wall (DW) dynamics, compared with their magnonic counterparts. By mapping the linear polarization dynamics of a DW onto a Schrödinger-like problem with a Pöschl-Teller potential, we show that polarization waves are fully transmitted and therefore do not exert a net force on the DW in the linear regime. However, intrinsic nonlinearities give rise to a negative radiation pressure that pulls the DW toward the source. This mechanism allows efficient DW control by optical excitation and temperature gradients with application potential in ferroelectric memory and logic devices.

AI.tldr: Ferroelectric domain wall dynamics driven by polarization currents via ferrons, showing linear transmission but nonlinear negative radiation pressure enabling optical/temperature control for memory/logic applications.
AI.motivation: To investigate the dynamics of ferroelectric textures driven by polarization currents, comparing ferrons (polarization quanta) with magnonic counterparts, and explore mechanisms for efficient domain wall control in ferroelectric devices.
AI.method: Mapping linear polarization dynamics of domain walls onto a Schrödinger-like problem with Pöschl-Teller potential to analyze transmission properties, then studying intrinsic nonlinearities that give rise to negative radiation pressure.
AI.result: Polarization waves are fully transmitted in linear regime (no net force on domain walls), but intrinsic nonlinearities create negative radiation pressure that pulls domain walls toward the source, enabling efficient control via optical excitation and temperature gradients.
AI.conclusion: Ferrons provide exotic driving mechanism for domain wall dynamics with negative radiation pressure effect, offering promising application potential in ferroelectric memory and logic devices through optical and thermal control mechanisms.

title: Theory of Many-Body Multipole Operators in Single-Centered Electron Systems: Two-Body Toroidal Monopoles in Spinless Orbitals
comment: 5 pages in the main text, plus 100 pages of supplemental material
summary: One-body multipole operators are defined as irreducible representations of rotational symmetry together with spatial-inversion and time-reversal symmetries, providing a systematic framework for classifying electronic internal degrees of freedom and for describing a wide variety of composite order parameters. While this formalism has been successfully established for the one-body operator space, a systematic classification of the many-body operator space, especially in interacting systems, remains an open challenge. In this paper, we extend the multipole formalism in the one-body operator space to the many-body operator space. By formulating fermionic creation and annihilation operators as spherical tensors and employing Clebsch-Gordan coupling combined with the exterior (Grassmann) algebra, we construct an irreducible decomposition of many-body operators that fully incorporates fermionic antisymmetrization. As a concrete application, we classify monopoles appearing in spinless many-body operators. In particular, we show that the electric toroidal monopole, a pseudoscalar breaking spatial-inversion symmetry, and the magnetic toroidal monopole, a time reversal-odd scalar, become active in spinless interacting many-body systems, although they are absent in the spinless one-body hybrid orbital space.

AI.tldr: Extension of multipole formalism from one-body to many-body operator space using fermionic spherical tensors and Clebsch-Gordan coupling with Grassmann algebra, enabling classification of many-body operators including monopoles in spinless systems.
AI.motivation: While one-body multipole operators are well-established for classifying electronic degrees of freedom and order parameters, there is no systematic classification of many-body operator space, especially in interacting systems, which limits the description of complex many-body phenomena.
AI.method: Formulate fermionic creation/annihilation operators as spherical tensors, employ Clebsch-Gordan coupling combined with exterior (Grassmann) algebra to construct irreducible decomposition of many-body operators that incorporates fermionic antisymmetrization.
AI.result: Successfully extended multipole formalism to many-body operator space. Classified monopoles in spinless many-body operators, showing that electric toroidal monopole (pseudoscalar breaking spatial-inversion symmetry) and magnetic toroidal monopole (time reversal-odd scalar) become active in spinless interacting many-body systems, despite being absent in spinless one-body hybrid orbital space.
AI.conclusion: The developed framework provides systematic classification of many-body operators, enabling description of complex many-body order parameters and revealing new types of monopoles that emerge only in interacting many-body systems, advancing the understanding of multipole physics beyond one-body approximations.

title: Beyond geometrical screening in predicting two-dimensional materials
summary: This perspective overviews the family of two-dimensional (2D) materials, which have attracted significant attention due to their properties and potential applications, and discusses how novel 2D materials including van der Waals (vdW) and non-vdW 2D materials have been predicted so far. A few thousand 2D materials have been predicted to be exfoliable or dynamically/thermodynamically stable, whereas a few hundred 2D materials have been synthesized so far, highlighting a gap between the theoretical prediction and experiments. This perspective introduces the recent developments in predicting the synthesis of non-vdW 2D materials.

AI.tldr: Overview of 2D materials family, highlighting the gap between theoretical predictions (thousands) and experimental synthesis (hundreds), with focus on recent developments in predicting synthesis of non-vdW 2D materials.
AI.motivation: To address the significant gap between the large number of theoretically predicted 2D materials (thousands) and the relatively small number that have been experimentally synthesized (hundreds), particularly focusing on non-van der Waals 2D materials which present unique synthesis challenges.
AI.method: Perspective review approach analyzing the family of 2D materials, including both van der Waals and non-vdW materials, examining prediction methods and synthesis approaches with emphasis on recent developments in computational prediction of non-vdW 2D material synthesis.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that while thousands of 2D materials have been predicted to be exfoliable or dynamically/thermodynamically stable, only a few hundred have been experimentally synthesized, creating a significant implementation gap that needs to be addressed through improved synthesis prediction methods.
AI.conclusion: Recent developments in predicting the synthesis of non-vdW 2D materials are crucial for bridging the gap between theoretical predictions and experimental realization, enabling the full potential of 2D materials to be realized in practical applications.

title: Non-Collinear and Non-Coplanar Magnetic Orders in 1/1 Periodic Approximant to the Icosahedral Quasicrystal
comment: 15 pages, 19 figures, Selected as JPSJ Editor's Choice, Selected as JPS Hot Topics
summary: Ground-state properties of rare-earth based 1/1 periodic approximants of icosahedral quasicrystal are clarified theoretically on the basis of an effective model for magnetism taking into account uniaxial anisotropy arising from crystalline electric field. By performing numerically-exact calculation on the 1/1 approximant crystal with a lattice constant $a$=14.725 Å, we have determined the ground-state phase diagram for ferromagnetic interactions. The result shows that eight kinds of noncollinear and noncoplanar magnetic structures are stabilized, whose magnetic space groups are identified as $I_{\rm P}m'\bar{3}'$, $C2'/m'$ and $R\bar{3}$. We have clarified the degeneracy of each ground state, which is expected to be reflected in the numbers of the domains. By analyzing each state, the magnetic as well as topological properties are revealed. Our results are shown to explain the measured magnetic structures in the 1/1 approximants and the effective model is discussed to be useful for understanding the magnetic structures and their topological properties in broad range of rare-earth based 1/1 approximants.

AI.tldr: Theoretical study reveals eight noncollinear/noncoplanar magnetic ground states in rare-earth 1/1 approximants with ferromagnetic interactions, explaining experimental observations and topological properties.
AI.motivation: To understand ground-state magnetic properties of rare-earth based 1/1 periodic approximants of icosahedral quasicrystals, particularly their magnetic structures and topological characteristics.
AI.method: Developed effective model incorporating uniaxial anisotropy from crystalline electric field, performed numerically-exact calculations on 1/1 approximant crystal with lattice constant a=14.725 Å, determined ground-state phase diagram for ferromagnetic interactions.
AI.result: Identified eight distinct noncollinear and noncoplanar magnetic structures with magnetic space groups I_Pm'3', C2'/m', and R3, clarified degeneracy of each ground state, analyzed magnetic and topological properties.
AI.conclusion: Results explain measured magnetic structures in 1/1 approximants; effective model is useful for understanding magnetic structures and topological properties across broad range of rare-earth based 1/1 approximants.

title: Microstructural Characterization of Nb3Sn Thin Films Using FIB Tomography
summary: The accelerating gradient of Nb3Sn superconducting radiofrequency (SRF) cavities is currently limited, and the underlying cause remains an open question in the field. One leading hypothesis attributes this limitation to the presence of tin-deficient regions within the Nb3Sn coating, which can suppress the superheating field. Due to the relatively large coherence length of Nb3Sn, defects near the surface may significantly interact with the RF field. However, these subsurface defects have proven difficult to characterize. This research aims to investigate the structure and distribution of subsurface Sn deficient regions to better understand their influence on cavity performance. We employ focused ion beam (FIB) tomography to analyze the subsurface microstructure of Nb3Sn thin films. This technique enables three-dimensional reconstruction of both the tin distribution and the grain structure within the film. By correlating Sn content with grain structure, we find that Sn deficient regions are more prevalent that previously thought. However, the Sn deficient regions are consistently located below the surface of the film where RF fields are strongly attenuated by supercurrent screening and are likely not a limiting factor for cavity performance.

AI.tldr: FIB tomography reveals that while Sn-deficient regions in Nb3Sn SRF coatings are more common than previously thought, they are located below the surface where RF fields are attenuated, suggesting they are not the primary performance limiter.
AI.motivation: The accelerating gradient of Nb3Sn SRF cavities is limited, with one leading hypothesis attributing this to tin-deficient regions suppressing the superheating field. These subsurface defects are difficult to characterize but may significantly interact with RF fields due to Nb3Sn's large coherence length.
AI.method: Focused ion beam (FIB) tomography is employed to analyze the subsurface microstructure of Nb3Sn thin films, enabling three-dimensional reconstruction of both tin distribution and grain structure within the film.
AI.result: Sn-deficient regions are more prevalent than previously thought, but they are consistently located below the film surface where RF fields are strongly attenuated by supercurrent screening, making them unlikely to be a limiting factor for cavity performance.
AI.conclusion: While Sn-deficient regions exist in Nb3Sn coatings, their subsurface location where RF fields are attenuated suggests they are not the primary cause of the accelerating gradient limitation in Nb3Sn SRF cavities.

title: Symmetry-directed electronic and optical properties in a two-dimensional square-lattice ZnPc-MOF
summary: The electronic structure of materials is fundamentally governed by their crystal symmetry. While most research on two-dimensional materials has focused on hexagonal lattices, such as graphene, hexagonal boron nitride, and transition metal dichalcogenides. This work explores a square-lattice system: the experimentally realized phthalocyanine-based metal-organic framework (ZnPc-MOF). Using group representation theory, we classify the electronic bands of ZnPc-MOF monolayer, AA- and AB-stacked bilayers, and twisted bilayers in terms of the irreducible representations (irreps) of their little groups. We find that bands in the AB-stacked bilayer remain two-fold degenerate along the $Y$ and $Y^{\prime}$ high-symmetry lines, as a consequence of the sole presence of two-dimensional irreps along these directions. We further derive optical transition selection rules to interpret the optical conductivity, revealing pronounced polarization-dependent optical responses. Additionally, we investigate the quasicrystalline electronic states in the 45$^{\circ}$ twisted bilayer (ZnPc-MOF quasicrystal) using the resonant coupling Hamiltonian. Compared to graphene quasicrystals, ZnPc-MOF quasicrystal exhibits weaker resonant coupling strengths, yet its quasicrystalline states lie closer to the Fermi energy, suggesting a greater contribution to low-energy electronic phenomena.

AI.tldr: Electronic structure analysis of square-lattice ZnPc-MOF using group theory reveals symmetry-protected degeneracies, polarization-dependent optical responses, and unique quasicrystalline states in twisted bilayers with stronger low-energy contributions than graphene quasicrystals.
AI.motivation: Most 2D materials research focuses on hexagonal lattices (graphene, hBN, TMDs), leaving square-lattice systems underexplored. This work investigates the electronic structure of experimentally realized ZnPc-MOF, a square-lattice metal-organic framework, to understand how crystal symmetry governs its electronic properties.
